title: CFP selection committee finally gets it right with Tennessee, Indiana rankings - CBS Sports
description: The Volunteers are getting the credit they deserve, while the Hoosiers finally got burned after weeks of playing
body:
The Volunteers are getting the credit they deserve, while the Hoosiers finally got burned after weeks of playing with fire
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:33 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The College Football Playoff selection committee finally did it.For the first time this season, the rankings…made sense. I wasn't filled with confusion and frustration over what the committee decided. Instead, the committee made decisions that seemed to emphasize resumes and metrics over ambiguous "eye test" considerations.Consider the big moves from this week:The committee finally ended its love affair with Alabama and moved the Crimson Tide three spots. It would have made sense to do so a week ago but credit the committee for acknowledging that Alabama's resume has taken a significant hit over the last month. With Kentucky and South Carolina dropping out of this week's rankings, Alabama is without a top-25 win and will presumably end its season without one against unranked Auburn in the Iron Bowl. With that move, the committee moved Texas to No. 3 (as predicted at CBS Sports) as the best two-loss team in the country. If Texas makes it to the SEC Championship and beats Georgia, it is an absolute lock for a top-four seed and first-round bye. Even if it loses to Georgia in the SEC title game, there's still a possibility it could finish in the top four depending on what happens elsewhere. 
Tennessee may not ever rank higher than its No. 5 spot Tuesday night, but it puts the Volunteers in prime position to host a playoff game. Earlier this week I called Neyland Stadium the greatest home-field advantage in college football, and it'd be a massive boon for the Vols to get one in Knoxville. There may not be a more ecstatic fanbase than Tennessee this week, after decrying Alabama's spot above the Volunteers for weeks. Mercifully for all of us, we won't have to discuss pods and groupings and whether head-to-head will be considered as much anymore with Alabama and Tennessee. Wake Forest is perhaps the hottest team in the country, and the committee has finally taken notice. The Demon Deacons jumped up to No. 8 from No. 10 a week ago. If those rankings hold for championship weekend, we'll get a No. 7 Miami versus No. 8 Wake Forest ACC Championship. Wake Forest is demolishing opponents and has the potential to keep moving up the rankings if it can win out. Conversely, Miami still has a chance to jump into that top four and get a bye as ACC champion. It would give the Hurricanes two wins over a very good Wake Forest team this season, and its lone loss coming to No. 4 Notre Dame. Indiana is not a playoff-caliber team at the moment, and the committee reflected that in the Hoosiers' six-spot drop. Was that too far a drop? Potentially. I predicted Indiana to land at No. 12 as the first team out rather than at No. 14 behind both Oregon and Iowa. Indiana has more top-25 wins and a better strength of schedule and strength of record than Iowa. The Hoosiers have a legitimate argument for being a spot too low. But I like the decision to rank Oregon, a team playing better football right now, above Indiana, especially with metrics like top-25 wins and strength of schedule to back up the decision. What does it mean for Indiana now? The Hoosiers' playoff hopes may heavily rely on not only making the Big Ten Championship but winning it. As it stands right now, if UCLA (vs. USC) and Oregon (vs. Washington) both win this weekend, the Hoosiers will be out of luck. And with a No. 14 ranking and only a potential win over Purdue left on the schedule, I don't see a particularly realistic path into the playoff field. It'd be a stunning miss for last year's national championship team. And, yet, after an egregiously bad non-conference schedule, it is perhaps deserved. Indiana's drop also increases the possibility of only one Big Ten team making the field. If UCLA, which dropped to No. 9 this week, loses to USC, the Bruins are out. Utah losing in the Big 12 title game could set up a scenario where three Big 12 teams make it (BYU and Texas Tech the others), four SEC teams make it, two ACC, Notre Dame, a Group of Six and then one of Oregon/Iowa/Indiana. The Big Ten bubble teams all need to be rooting for Utah to keep winning out and for BYU or Texas Tech to drop another game this weekend.I like how the committee handled the bottom of the top 25, too. Boise State missing the cut was a slight surprise but speaks to how much the Broncos' margin for error narrowed after a loss to San Diego State. Boise State still should be in if it wins out. After lots of public criticism over the number of four-loss SEC teams a week ago, the committee included a pair of Big Ten teams, Washington and Nebraska, that scored big wins last weekend. Washington and Nebraska are both deserving of spots 24 and 25. Ohio State's drop to No 21 feels fair, as well, given the Buckeyes' wins over Indiana and Iowa.It's easy to criticize the selection committee each week for failing at an impossible task of ranking the top 25 teams. In fact, this space is usually reserved for pointing out the teams that the committee either over- or under-rated. 
But if we're quick to criticize, we should also commend when appropriate. For one week, at least, this committee got it right.

title: Michigan matches worst start by reigning national champion in last 40 years: Why pressure is on Mike Boynton - CBS Sports
description: The Wolverines will need to turn things around quickly or Boynton won't be back for a second season
body:
The Wolverines will need to turn things around quickly or Boynton won't be back for a second season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    8:59 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Michigan dropped to 3-3 on Tuesday with a 99-73 loss to Creighton in its opening game of the Players Era 16, matching its loss total from last season's national title team. The Wolverines are now tied for the worst six-game start by the winner of the previous season's NCAA Tournament in the last 40 seasons.The only other reigning national champions that started 3-3 during that stretch? UConn (2014-15), UCLA (1995-96) and Louisville (1986-87). Michigan never lost back-to-back games against unranked teams during Dusty May's tenure as coach. The Wolverines now have losses on their resume against UConn, Villanova and Creighton.And it's not just that Michigan lost; it's how it happened. The 59 points Michigan allowed in the first half against Creighton were the most the program has allowed in a first half in 22 years (2004 vs. Georgia Tech). The 26-point defeat was Michigan's largest loss in nearly two years and the most points it allowed in a game since Jan. 2024 (vs. Purdue).
        
            
                College basketball rankings: Keep an eye on the 5-0 Ole Miss Rebels scratching right outside the Top 25 And 1
                
                    Gary Parrish                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
More context on why this loss is so stunning: Last year, at this same tournament, Michigan announced itself as a legit national title contender. The Wolverines beat San Diego State by 40, defeated Auburn by 30 and Gonzaga by 40 in the title game. Michigan's third loss that season didn't come until the Big Ten Tournament title game against Purdue on Selection Sunday.Why the pressure is on Mike BoyntonWhen May unexpectedly stepped down and took the job with the Mavericks, it sent shock waves throughout the sport. Michigan was able to keep its roster together by promoting Mike Boynton, who served as the team's lead assistant and defensive coordinator last season.
So far, the returns for the former Oklahoma State coach have not been positive. Boynton, who signed a two-year contract with the school — with the second season not guaranteed — has to meet certain benchmarks to ensure his return next season. Here are those requirements. Notable: If Michigan reaches the Final Four, the requirements are satisfied. Win 24 regular-season gamesFinish in the top four of the Big Ten regular-season standingsWin the Big Ten Tournament Reach the Sweet 16 of the NCAA Tournament Boynton is making $3.6 million this season and would make $4 million during the 2027-28 season if he is retained. Michigan is currently searching for a new athletic director after the school announced it would not be hiring former Texas A&M AD Trev Alberts for the role after all.
The Wolverines dropped out of the AP Top 25 poll after a loss against Villanova last week on the road. After losing to Creighton in blowout fashion, the pressure is mounting to get back on track ahead of a stretch that includes a matchup Thursday against No. 17 Miami in the losers bracket of the Players Era 16.

title: Jalen Davis commits to Gonzaga: Bulldogs land the No. 13-ranked prospect in 2027 class - CBS Sports
description: Davis is Gonzaga's second commitment for this cycle
body:
Davis is Gonzaga's second commitment for this cycle
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:40 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Four-star combo guard Jalen Davis committed to Gonzaga on CBS Sports HQ on Tuesday. The No. 13-ranked player in the 2027 recruiting cycle by 247Sports committed to the Bulldogs over North Carolina, UCLA and Washington.The Bremerton, Washington, product is Gonzaga's second commitment of the 2027 recruiting cycle, joining four-star guard Dooney Johnson. Johnson is ranked the No. 30 prospect In the 2027 class
If Davis and Johnson end up signing with the Bulldogs, it would mark the first time since 2021 that the program landed two top-30 commitments in the same recruiting cycle. That year, Gonzaga signed Chet Holmgren (No. 1 overall) and Hunter Sallis (No. 10 overall). Davis is the highest-ranked commitment Gonzaga has landed since that star-studded class.
247Sports Director of Scouting Adam Finklestein says Davis' "processing ability" is what sets him apart."Davis is a skilled guard who differentiates himself with his feel for the game, processing ability, and understanding of how to be a high-volume scorer without having to dominate the basketball. He put up over 23 points per game in the 3SSB season, on over 49% shooting from the floor, while playing largely off the ball. He moves without the ball extremely well. He's a good cutter, knows how to use screens, and is still a very effective passer. There aren't many players in high school basketball who can read a pin-down and then make a pocket pass if the big helps on his catch, but Davis is one of them. His ability to make quick reads and decisions is one of the most impressive parts of his game."There has been a flood of big-name commitments from the 2027 recruiting cycle during the last several weeks. On Monday, five-star CJ Rosser committed to North Carolina, which marked the highest-ranked player from the upcoming recruiting cycle to come off the board.
Other notable names who have come off the board: DeMarcus Henry (North Carolina), Lewis Uvwo (Providence), Reese Alston (LSU), Asa Montgomery (Duke) and Cayden Daughtry (Arkansas). Notably, Beckham Black, the No. 1-ranked player in the 2027 recruiting class, has yet to announce where he will be playing next season.

body:
Dobbins will not play against the Steelers on Friday as Denver holds a slight lead over Kansas City in the AFC West race
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:07 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
            
        
                
                
                
            
        
            
                    
                Getty Images
            
            

    
        The Denver Broncos will play their Week 12 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers without running back J.K. Dobbins. Coach Sean Payton announced that he suspended the veteran ball carrier for one game for conduct detrimental to the team, which takes him out of the offensive rotation for the Black Friday contest. Payton did not comment further on the suspension or what prompted his decision, adding that "it's better that way" to not speak on the matter.Although Dobbins leads the team in carries (99) and rushing yards (324), with three touchdowns on his ledger this season, he slipped in the pecking order in recent weeks behind RJ Harvey and rookie Jonah Coleman. Dobbins' role reached a new low in last week's win over the Las Vegas Raiders when he played just one snap.Coleman emerged as the primary option in the backfield and took firm command of the starting job when he set career highs with 28 touches, 129 scrimmage yards and three touchdowns in that victory against the Raiders.Harvey is on injured reserve due to a knee issue that popped up in practice in late October. He will not play on Friday and is not eligible to return until Week 13 against the Miami Dolphins.
With two of the top three running backs out for the matchup with the Steelers, Coleman projects to take on a sizable workload for the second time in as many weeks. Payton declined to answer questions about the group but insisted that the Broncos will have depth at the position. If anyone steps into a more meaningful role, it would likely be Cody Schrader, whom the Broncos activated to their 53-man roster for each of the last three games. Tyler Badie's practice window is open, but the Broncos have not activated him from injured reserve.

body:
RJ Luis Jr. played one game at LSU last week. Now it might end LSU's nearly 100-year membership in the Southeastern Conference.A months-long battle between the SEC and LSU over the school's decision to roster former professional players in basketball and football has reached a breaking point. For the second time this fall, the SEC has scheduled a vote to expel LSU, and the league doesn't appear willing to back down after saying school officials misled the conference and decided to play a former NBA player in a Nov. 18 nonconference game against Louisiana-Monroe.In its Nov. 23 federal court filing, the league claims LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry and men's basketball coach Will Wade both told SEC commissioner Greg Sankey that Luis would not actually play for the Tigers. A Baton Rouge judge cleared the way on Nov. 13, granting Luis a preliminary injunction that barred the SEC and NCAA from punishing LSU for playing him. LSU put him on the roster four days later.Around the SEC, the outrage included discussions about potentially boycotting LSU games, CBS Sports' Matt Norlander and John Talty reported. Then, Wade played Luis anyway. A day later, Sankey phoned LSU president Wade Rousse, and Rousse announced the Tigers would no longer allow Luis to play in games. Luis has since left the program, but his lawyer is now threatening a lawsuit against the SEC and commissioner Greg Sankey.
The SEC's presidents, who had grown tired of LSU's actions, weren't interested in the school's latest retreat. Five days later, the SEC filed another document in federal court in Birmingham, Alabama, announcing its intention to hold a Dec. 3 vote on LSU's membership.
        
            
                SEC schedules vote on possible LSU expulsion as RJ Luis dispute pushes league to the brink
                
                    John Talty                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
It takes 11 votes from the league's 16 presidents and chancellors to end LSU's membership in a conference it helped start in 1932. Rousse will get a vote in an attempt to block expulsion.The SEC has never kicked out a member of its league. The closest modern precedent in major college athletics is Temple, which the Big East removed after the 2004 season because the program failed to reach minimum membership standards -- not for blatant disregard of league rules.
The road here has been long and filled with legal filings and public callouts. In September, the league scheduled a meeting to consider terminating LSU's membership as Lane Kiffin's football program pursued three former NFL players: former Browns tight end Dae'Quan Wright, former Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton. Sources told CBS Sports in August that the votes to expel LSU were secured if the school wasn't willing to back down. LSU backed down, leaving Wright and Harris off its 105-player roster. The scheduled meeting ended without sanctions.The latest move by LSU in basketball, along with public criticism from public officials, has angered SEC presidents, multiple sources told CBS Sports. Expulsion is still considered unlikely, but there is enough frustration among the presidents and chancellors, those sources said, that at least some could be in favor of voting LSU out."Greg Sankey is only acting on what he knows to be the will of the majority. He would not allow this initiative to proceed if he wasn't sure he had the votes," former Big 12 commissioner Bob Bowlsby told CBS Sports.
The fight is no longer about one basketball player, or two football players, or even LSU. It is about whether a conference can still make its members follow its rules. It's particularly paramount as the Protect College Sports Act, a bill that would provide antitrust protections allowing conferences to enforce rules, flounders in the House of Representatives.Why the SEC has to draw the lineThe rule LSU is accused of breaking is one LSU helped write.On Aug. 25, all 16 SEC chief executives, including Rousse, voted on a policy statement regarding the rostering of former professional athletes, according to the SEC's amended federal complaint. Rousse abstained on the penalty memo that followed. The penalties on the table were stiff: a half-season suspension for the head coach, a fine of up to 50% of a sport's annual budget and the loss of voting privileges.The football players sued in state court in East Baton Rouge Parish on Aug. 19. Luis won his injunction in the same courthouse in November. In its latest filing this week, the SEC argues those rulings leave it boxed in, writing that the "SEC has no avenue to penalize LSU." 
The league said it would abide by the Louisiana order and "not impose penalties or fines on LSU" for rostering Luis, CBS Sports reported. The SEC also alleges that "defendants are actively collaborating with third party professional athletes to defy SEC rules." "College sports, frankly, is a culture of breaking rules right now -- one can say it always has been, but it's hard to see a rule as binding when it's so easy to file and win a lawsuit to overcome it," said Sam Ehrlich, a sports law scholar at Boise State. "And since as we're discovering a lot of that can be attributed to the simple fact that so many of the rules in question are just blatantly illegal, schools, players and their attorneys clearly see boundary testing as necessary. If they don't, someone else will and get an advantage based on that."So I'm sure LSU just sees this as them getting punished for conduct that everyone else is doing."
The SEC's argument is simple: the conference creates its own rules, and those who violate those rules are subject to punishment. In court, LSU argues that the rules don't apply to it and that the courts hold authority.The SEC's federal lawsuit rests on a First Amendment claim of freedom of association."The lawsuit seeks to protect the Conference's ability to govern itself," the SEC said in a statement. "The Conference maintains its right to associate only with institutions that meet its established standards."
Think of the SEC as a Homeowners Association, noted sports attorney Tom Mars explained this week."Legally speaking, the SEC is no different than an HOA and can take whatever actions against its members its bylaws allow it to take, which for the SEC, includes expulsion," Mars said on X. "Much like dealing with a disruptive HOA resident who refuses to follow the HOA bylaws, I don't understand why the SEC Presidents don't vote to conditionally disassociate LSU from the league within the next 10 days (or some other reasonable time period) unless LSU takes certain specified actions to satisfy the SEC that LSU will stop ignoring its rules, being disruptive, and creating chaos for its members."Mars agreed that the SEC doesn't want to boot LSU from the conference, but disassociating from the school could force LSU to decide on its own whether to remain a member of the SEC.
"Problem solved," Mars said.Pressure is coming from outside the league office, too. On Nov. 18, Georgia Attorney General Christopher Carr sent a letter urging sanctions "up to and including expulsion," ESPN reported.A catalyst to end conferences?The answer that could settle all of this sits on Capitol Hill.The Protect College Sports Act is expected to reach the House floor on Dec. 8, five days after the SEC's vote on LSU. The bill would provide targeted antitrust protections for conferences and similar organizations, including in players' eligibility cases.The bill's chances of passing the House -- and potentially through the Senate again if revisions are made -- before a new Congress is sworn in in January are slim, sources said. If it doesn't become law, that leaves the conferences in position to enforce stricter rules, though those will continue to be challenged in court without the PCSA's protection.
"But if the PCSA doesn't pass, the future might just have to be single conference governance, and I'm sure the SEC sees this as a test balloon, and a situation where they need to assert themselves hard when you have such a blatant rule violation," Ehrlich said. "I'd imagine they think that if they don't, they'll just be another NCAA moving forward -- an entity that has lost all of its enforcement teeth."Another issue is clearly outlined in the bill: any previous or ongoing cases would not be subject to the PCSA's provisions. That includes the LSU and SEC cases.Still, conferences hold the threat of power because they can simplify scheduling opportunities, championship events and increase media revenue for their membership.
NCAA automatic qualifications in every sport run through conferences. The money runs through them, too. The SEC distributed $1.03 billion to its 16 schools for the 2024-25 fiscal year, and its ESPN deal runs through 2034 at a reported $300 million per year.A school that walks away from a conference -- or is pushed out -- gives up all of that.That makes Dec. 3 a test of whether a conference can still act like one. If a member can stay in by court order while ignoring the rules, the conference starts to look like a toothless organization that spends millions in court trying to enforce rules some judges view as unlawful. It's the same problem the NCAA has faced over the last five years, leading to a slew of losses in court and the landmark House v. NCAA settlement that opened the door for players to be paid in revenue sharing.LSU as an independent?Money motivates change more than anything in college sports. The question is: could LSU financially afford to go it alone if it were expelled from the SEC or chose to leave the conference on its own?If LSU were expelled, it would immediately lose its right to future revenue distributions from the SEC, according to the league's constitution. LSU received $72.4 million in conference and NCAA distributions in 2025, according to athletics data provided to the Knight Commission. The SEC shared $69.5 million in conference-related payments, including $53.1 million in media rights revenue, according to LSU's financial report to the NCAA for the 2025 fiscal year. LSU's athletic department is among the nation's richest, bringing in $223.5 million in revenue that same year, according to the report. LSU could sue the SEC for breach of its membership agreement and seek any distribution already due, said Scott Schneider, a Texas law professor. If LSU proved it was wrongfully expelled, he said, it could seek the distributions it actually lost, accounting for replacement revenue.Schneider pointed to the Metro Conference in 1995, when five schools voted to remove Virginia Tech and VCU. Virginia Tech and VCU sought an injunction, arguing the five universities had effectively withdrawn to form a new conference and had lost the right to cast the votes that expelled them. The two schools split a $2.27 million settlement over conference revenue. It illustrates how LSU might build a financial claim around a defect in the vote, Schneider said, though it leaves open what a court would actually award financially.Without a partnership with the SEC, LSU would have to schedule games on its own and secure new media partnerships as an independent. SEC members would assuredly be blocked from scheduling games with LSU, and many teams in other leagues have already filled their schedules for the foreseeable future.If LSU tried to find a landing spot in another conference, suitors could be placed in an impossible situation with a program that has already shown its unwillingness to follow a conference's rulebook. Industry sources believe the Big Ten would not show immediate interest in adding LSU after its fight with the SEC. That leaves the Big 12, the ACC or independence, with conference membership not guaranteed.On its own, LSU's product has proven drawing power. LSU averaged 5.95 million viewers across eight charted games through the first 11 weeks of the college football season, ranking third nationally behind Texas and Alabama, according to data compiled by CBS Sports via available Nielsen ratings.LSU's Sept. 19 game at Ole Miss drew 10.9 million viewers, the third-largest audience of the season.But that is also the problem: LSU's highest-rated games are against SEC rivals. LSU's three biggest audiences came against Ole Miss, Texas and Alabama. That is the inventory an independent LSU would have to replace, with opponents that would have to agree to play the Tigers.LSU is assured at least nine games as an SEC member."I'm not sure there's going to be enough quality games out there to make them an attractive standalone television property," said former Fox Sports Network president Bob Thompson. "Certainly not one that will generate more revenue than they currently receive from the SEC."Which team would agree to schedule LSU in November if it is trying to remain undefeated late in a season?  "Seems as though [LSU] might have to write some large checks to fill out a 12-game schedule," Thompson surmised.LSU paid $4.5 million to non-conference teams during the 2025 fiscal year. An independent LSU would have to fill a 12-game football schedule, as well as hundreds of events for all 21 of its sports.The other obvious model LSU could attempt to mimic is Notre Dame. Its NBC deal runs through 2029, with games on NBC and Peacock. The value has never been disclosed, though the Sports Business Journal reported in 2022 that it was expected to fetch about $60 million per year.Notre Dame, however, is not completely independent. Nearly all of the school's other sports aside from football are housed under the ACC banner. The football program also has a five-game scheduling agreement with the ACC through 2037.An independent LSU would also have no access to conference tournaments or an automatic NCAA bid in any sport, leaving its high-powered baseball, basketball and gymnastics programs to chase at-large bids. The nearest example is Oregon State baseball, which played as a Division I independent in 2025 and 2026 after the Pac-12 collapsed. Postseason access for LSU in football is also unclear. Notre Dame is the only independent written into the College Football Playoff's selection process by name, with an automatic bid if it finishes in the top 12. An independent LSU would be an at-large candidate under the current format."Key question at that point would be whether LSU would join another conference or try it as an independent," Ehrlich said.The courtroom clockA vote to expel LSU would likely not be the last word, according to legal experts. The expectation is LSU would seek an immediate court order preserving its SEC membership.Meanwhile, the SEC has already chosen a courtroom in its backyard of Birmingham, Alabama. Its lawsuit against LSU officials sits in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Alabama before Judge Annemarie Carney Axon. The SEC sued Rousse, Ausberry, Kiffin, members of the LSU board and Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill in their official capacities, a structure that appears designed to circumvent state sovereign immunity.The defendants' motion to dismiss, filed Sept. 25, has not been ruled on. On Nov. 23, the SEC filed a new motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to get the judge's nod to continue its deliberations on LSU's future. A hearing on that motion is set for Wednesday in Birmingham.The Birmingham judge has already shown impatience with LSU's side. At a Nov. 18 hearing, she ordered LSU's lawyers to retract a page in a filing and apologize for accusing the SEC's counsel of "hallucinated" citations."You put the pig out there, there's no time to put lipstick on it," Axon said, according to the Tuscaloosa News.LSU's friendlier venue is in Baton Rouge, where Judge William Jorden of the 19th Judicial District Court granted Luis' injunction. Louisiana law allows a temporary restraining order on a showing of immediate, irreparable harm. And given two prior rulings there against SEC penalties, a quick order keeping LSU in the league pending a hearing is plausible. In Schneider's opinion, neither existing Louisiana order expressly bars expulsion, though LSU could argue the vote was a penalty solely for playing Luis."The SEC would point to what happened across two sports and ask whether the other presidents can rely on LSU to enforce a rule its own president supported. That institutional control argument is why the reasons the presidents give for their vote matter," Schneider said.That prompts another question for legal scholars that only the courts can answer: Whether a state court order could hold against a conflicting federal one.If a federal court entered a final judgment upholding LSU's expulsion, Schneider's best guess is that it would bind the parties on the issues, so LSU couldn't ask a Louisiana judge to decide those same issues in the school's favor. If a Louisiana judge had already blocked the expulsion, though, that injunction wouldn't disappear automatically, he said. The SEC would then take the federal judgment back to that judge and ask that it be lifted.That scenario is a hypothetical. The SEC hasn't asked Axon to uphold an expulsion, Schneider noted. The SEC's most recent motion seeks to keep LSU officials from blocking the Dec. 3 meeting or undoing its outcome in another court, and it expressly preserves their right to challenge an expulsion in the Birmingham court in the SEC's backyard."The SEC could win this motion in full and still lose a later challenge to the presidents' vote," Schneider said.
        
            
                LSU's RJ Luis planning to sue SEC, Greg Sankey over eligibility drama
                
                    Brad Crawford                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Then there is Luis himself. His attorney, Tony Clayton, said Monday Luis will sue the SEC and Sankey for damages and depose every SEC president."Mr. Sankey will feel the wrath of RJ Luis, if not by Christmas, then by New Year's night," Clayton told ESPN.The school and the league could reach an amicable resolution, CBS Sports reported Monday, but only if LSU provides tangible evidence and good-faith actions showing it will abide by all league rules going forward. One likely mandate is concrete assurance that "Louisiana governor Jeff Landry's influence over certain athletics matters will no longer determine how the university conducts itself under the SEC's bylaws."History suggests these fights will end at the negotiating table. The question is whether LSU would accept other punishments short of expulsion. If not, those negotiations may continue through legal filings, as has happened elsewhere.In November 2023, Washington State and Oregon State won control of the Pac-12 in a home-state court after a four-month battle. Florida State and Clemson settled with the ACC in March 2025 after a year-long battle concerning the schools' ability to leave the conference without paying nine-figure exit fees. But past results likely don't apply to the SEC's family feud. This dispute is beyond precedent.

Texas and Notre Dame slide into the top four while the Big 12 lands three teams in the projected 12-team field after UCLA's loss shook up the rankings

        No. 3 Texas jumped into the first-round byes after obliterating Arkansas over the weekend, reshuffling the College Football Playoff bracket after four weeks. The Longhorns and No. 4 Notre Dame both moved into the top group after UCLA's loss, and finally moved past Alabama as the Tide's best wins atrophy. No. 1 Georgia and No. 2 Utah held the top spots on the board, with No. 5 Tennessee moving into the first home host of the first round. They'd be projected to play 12-seed Boise State in the first round. The Crimson Tide sit at No. 6 with No. 7 Miami and No. 8 Wake Forest lurking close behind. The Big 12 was a major winner of the most recent bracket as No. 10 BYU and No. 11 Texas Tech both remained in the bracket, giving the league a shot at three teams. No. 9 UCLA went from a first round bye to traveling on the road to play Wake Forest in the projected bracket. No. 12 Oregon and No. 13 Iowa rank as the first two teams out of the field. Here is how the College Football Playoff bracket looks after the fourth CFP Rankings release of the 2026 season. 

                                                                    CBS Sports Graphic
                                                            Big Ten in troubleIf the season ended today, the Big Ten would -- amazingly -- only get one team in the field. No. 9 UCLA is the only team projected in the bracket, and the Bruins are heavy underdogs against USC this weekend. That said, the first four teams out of the field as it stands are all from the Big Ten, including No. 12 Oregon, No. 13 Iowa and No. 14 Indiana. There's still a pathway for each to work their way back, but they need some luck to go their way. Even so, it's very realistic that the league could only send its champion to the postseason, a stunning failure for the conference that produced the last three national champions. Alabama finally dropsHeading into this week, Alabama was rated as the No. 3 team in the nation despite a schedule that didn't pass muster. The Crimson Tide have not beaten a team with a record better than 7-4, and haven't beaten a team of even that caliber since September. 
After Kentucky fell again over the weekend, the committee finally punished the Crimson Tide. Alabama is down to No. 6 in the rankings, behind No. 3 Texas and No. 5 Tennessee from the SEC. The Volunteers have a head-to-head win by two touchdowns in Neyland Stadium and finally jumped ahead.

body:
Duke is out to avenge that gut-wrenching Elite Eight loss to UConn, but most importantly, Scheyer's club has to get right

        Duke basketball has been in the news for all the wrong reasons after getting clubbed by both Michigan State and Illinois. The Blue Devils look far from a National Championship contender at this juncture, but the daunting tests keep on coming. That's the beauty (or curse) of cobbling together the best nonconference schedule in the land. Duke now has to step into the Las Vegas octagon and face No. 10 UConn, who took Duke's soul last March in an epic Elite Eight game that no one will forget anytime soon.Avenging that gut-wrenching loss is the easy storyline, but Duke is far more focused on trying to find itself. That's easier said than done against a UConn team that might be short-handed but is still playing a brand of basketball that Dan Hurley loves. 
        
            
                College basketball rankings: Keep an eye on the 5-0 Ole Miss Rebels scratching right outside the Top 25 And 1
                
                    Gary Parrish                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Let's dive into the nuts and bolts of this matchup. Duke vs. UConn: Need to knowJon Scheyer's tweaks: Duke changed the starting lineup ahead of a shaky win over Washington State on Saturday, inserting Sebastian Wilkins and Caleb Foster into the lineup for Dame Sarr and Cayden Boozer, respectively. Duke also ditched a lot of its soft switches to try and play with a bit more bite after getting taken to the woodshed by Illinois' offensive flamethrowing duo of Andrej Stojakovic and Quentin Coleman. You know what else would help? Making shots. Duke is shooting just 28% from 3-point range through six games. A lot of problems can go away if a sniper like John Blackwell can get it rolling.Braylon Mullins is a problem: Mullins' historic, last-second shot against Duke is his most famous moment. He's also a way, way better basketball player this season. The rising sophomore is averaging north of 20 points per game and draining 38% of his 3-pointers. Mullins looks stronger and far more assertive. UConn is also playing with a bit more pace which has helped Mullins get more cleaner transition looks. He's one of the best players in the country. Duke has to turn his water off.
The juicy Nik Khamenia storyline is not meant to be: Khamenia ruffled more than a few feathers when the former 5-star forward transferred from Duke to UConn in the spring. title: Why asking Trae Young to score less is a band-aid, not a fix for the Wizards' self-inflicted problem - CBS Sports
description: Young has been a mess as a scorer this season, shooting just 36.4% from the floor and 32.5% on 3s
body:
Young has been a mess as a scorer this season, shooting just 36.4% from the floor and 32.5% on 3s
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    8:55 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Washington Wizards entered Tuesday with a 7-11 record. In their seven wins, Trae Young is averaging just under 11.3 shot attempts per game. In those 11 losses, he's averaging 13.3. It's a small difference, but a notable one. The Wizards came into play Tuesday on a three-game winning streak, and a meaningful part of that streak has been Young spending less time on the ball. In Washington's first 15 games, he averaged around 6.6 minutes of possession per game, tied for the third-most in the league. He's down to 4.5 in his last three games. He's dribbling around one fewer time per touch, and his average possession per touch is down around a second. These aren't glaring changes, but they've been helpful ones. It's not a coincidence, for example, that No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa's two best offensive games have come in this stretch. Young, 28, has been a mess as a scorer this season. He's shooting just 36.4% from the floor and 32.5% on 3s. He's barely getting to the basket and struggling mightily when he's in the paint. He can't beat defenders nearly as easily off the dribble as he once could. Getting the ball out of his hands a bit more has been essential. 
It's been an intentional shift on Washington's part. Wizards officials have asked Young to focus less on his own scoring and instead emphasize his playmaking, according to The Athletic. Washington certainly won't complain about a 24-to-7 assist-to-turnover ratio in that stretch. Young, despite his noticeable decline as a scorer, remains a stellar passer. That's typically how star decline works. It comes in bits and pieces. Even as essential components of a player's game degrade, years of accumulated basketball IQ allow him to continue finding ways to contribute. After years of abject tanking, the Wizards seemingly wanted an offensive organizer around to help give their younger players some structure. Young can still do that.
But we're in an increasingly financially unforgiving NBA, and the Wizards aren't paying Young a contributor's salary. They're paying him star money, and they chose to do so after just five relatively quiet games with him a season ago. His four-year, $212 million max contract will pay him at the top of the market through the end of Dybantsa's rookie deal. With Anthony Davis on the books through the end of Kyshawn George and Alex Sarr's rookie deals, the Wizards effectively traded the roster-building flexibility those cheap rookie deals afforded them for two declining stars. Davis has justified the investment, at least as an asset. They haven't extended him. They could potentially flip him for more than they paid him. Young has not.And that's the dilemma the Wizards are now in. 
        
            
                NBA Hater Report: Celtics can't shoot, neither can Trae Young and James Harden isn't close to a top 10 player
                
                    Brad Botkin                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
A daunting shift for YoungClearly, less Young leads to more winning for the Wizards. But getting enough out of him to justify that enormous contract almost certainly requires more than they're currently getting. The entire value proposition of employing Young rests on him being a high-usage offensive engine. He just doesn't provide enough off-ball offensive value to justify what he gives up defensively at a max price point.
Take his shooting, for example. "Trae's got so much gravity," Wizards coach Brian Keefe told The Athletic. "When he plays off the ball, he's going to draw people, and then we're getting into actions with him on the second side that have been really good." There's something to this in theory, especially since gravity tends to rest more on reputation than reality. But Young has never been a consistently reliable catch-and-shoot player. He's averaging less than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game this season and has made around 28% of them. He's never averaged more than two catch-and-shoot 3-point attempts per game in a season. Maybe he improves if his role demands more of these shots, but this is his ninth NBA season. That sort of shift this late in a career is rare.It's a daunting change. Young spent most of his seven-and-a-half-year Atlanta Hawks run as almost entirely an on-ball player. He's never scored more than 39 points off of cuts in a single season. He has none this season. He's never been an especially active mover or screener, and even if he's grown on that front over the last few years, that's from a starting point of essentially zero. Asking Young to be less of a heliocentric shot creator is essentially asking Young to be a different player entirely.
That was the danger in paying Young sight unseen. They had no idea how he'd fit on this roster when they ponied up a max deal. If he'd picked up his player option and made this a prove-it season, they could have worked out the kinks and tried to sign him to a more appropriate deal next summer. The obvious argument here is that Young might have left had the Wizards refused to give him a long-term extension, but the counter here is that the Wizards would almost certainly have been better off if that had happened. Stephen Noh's salary model estimates that Young is worth $26.3 million so far this season. That's a bit less than half of what he's getting. If that persists over the life of the deal, it's among the NBA's worst contracts. If his scoring continues to decline as he loses burst with age, it's a borderline crisis. Young may remain a passing genius, but passing skill is not a one-to-one match with passing value. It's easier to set teammates up when you're a dangerous enough scorer to consistently draw help. If Young isn't generating the same sort of advantages he once did, the passes that were once available to him suddenly become harder.All of this puts the Wizards in an extremely precarious long-term position. They had to get the ball out of Young's hands more in the present. Too much of their offense involved players more important to the organization's long-term plans -- Dybantsa chief among them -- watching him dribble. A lower-usage Young probably makes the Wizards a better team simply by spreading usage to players who need more of it. 
But that doesn't mean that a lower-usage Young is especially valuable. On-ball creation is where much of Young's value is generated. His scoring has declined so much that he's not generating the same value he used to, so all of this has stuck the Wizards between a rock and a hard place. They can try to maximize Young's skill set at the expense of everyone else, or they can try to maximize the team as a whole. But in doing so, they're not getting nearly enough out of a player they're paying to be a centerpiece. The latter is probably the right decision, but it's still a choice between two bad options. It's a band-aid on a self-inflicted wound.

title: MLB rumors: Corey Seager willing to waive his NTC for Phillies, plus news on Mets, Nationals, Yankees, more - CBS Sports
description: Here are your offseason hot stove rumors on Tuesday, Nov. 24
body:
Here are your offseason hot stove rumors on Tuesday, Nov. 24
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 24, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:02 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22, and this time around we've already seen some leading examples. Just recently, for instance, the New York Mets landed the biggest fish in the pond by signing ace Tarik Skubal to a record contract. Not long after, the Chicago Cubs fortified their rotation with Trevor Rogers and their outfield with Teruaki Sato, and Freddy Peralta is headed to the Baltimore Orioles. More's surely to come before lockout day arrives. Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Tuesday's supply just below. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Stephenson returns to Reds
Free agent catcher Tyler Stephenson has agreed to a three-year contract to return to the Reds, reports ESPN. The deal is worth $30 million and includes an opt-out after the second year. Cincinnati selected Stephenson, 30, with the No. 11 pick in the 2015 draft, and he's played his entire career with the Reds. We ranked him as the 46th-best free agent available.The Reds will again pair Stephenson with glove-first backup Jose Trevino behind the plate. Cincinnati now figures to turn their attention to the pitching staff, both the rotation and bullpen. Hunter Greene's UCL surgery means Andrew Abbott and Chase Burns are the only locks for the rotation, though Nick Lodolo will have a spot as long as he's healthy.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Yankees interested in Morejon; Phillies out?
The Yankees are among the many teams with interest in top free agent reliever Adrian Morejon, reports the New York Post. Some teams view him as a potential starter, though there were reports earlier this month that he prefers to stay in the bullpen. The Phillies, meanwhile, are not considered a serious candidate to sign Morejon, according to The Athletic. We ranked him as the second-best free agent available this offseason, in part due to his potential to start.Adding to the bullpen has been the Yankees' primary focus so far this offseason. Closer David Bednar accepted the qualifying offer, they re-signed lefty matchup guy Tim Hill, and signed Jonathan Loáisiga and Tim Hill as free agents. At some point they will need to add to their lineup, particularly at third base, but there's always room for a reliever like Morejon in the bullpen.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Corey Seager willing to waive no-trade clause to join Phillies
The Philadelphia Phillies are open to moving Trea Turner off of shortstop given that he's now a pronounced defensive liability. Speaking of openness, veteran shortstop Corey Seager of the Texas Rangers is willing to waive his no-trade clause to join the Phillies and upgrade the position for them, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports.
Now 32, Seager will always have health and durability concerns, but he remains a plus defensive shortstop who produces well at the plate by positional standards. Signed to a 10-year, $325 million deal prior to the 2022 season (just before the last lockout, in fact), Seager is owed another $155 million through the 2031 season. The Rangers are reportedly looking to shake things up. The Phillies, meantime, are trying to keep their contention window open. It's a fit both ways, at least in theory. Such a move would likely mean a move to the outfield for Turner, who himself has very little trade value thanks to his ongoing decline and big contract. Jazz Chisholm Jr. market picking up
Even in a down 2026 year, Jazz Chisholm Jr. put up 19 homers and stole 41 bases while manning an up-the-middle position. Still just 28 years of age, he figures to have a healthy market this offseason. Speaking of which, the Washington Nationals are one of multiple teams presently in contact with Chisholm, FanSided reports. Earlier in the offseason, CBS Sports ranked Chisholm as the No. 6 free agent in the current class. Here's part of that write-up: 
"In what was his worst season as a hitter since his rookie year in 2021, Chisholm was still a league-average bat in 2026, and his top-shelf defense and baserunning still landed him at 3.5 WAR. Chisholm is a style-over-substance player who is not for everyone, but his second base defense and near-MLB-best baserunning skills give him a very high floor. He's a reasonable bet for 20-ish home runs with the potential to go 30-30, and Chisholm has improved his plate discipline enough to run walk rates north of 10% the last two years. The downside is his propensity to swing and miss. Chisholm has posted below-average in-zone contact rates throughout his career and contact rates that low always come with risk. That risk is mitigated somewhat by the secondary skills (defense, etc.) and the fact that Chisholm will play the entire 2027 season at age 29. You probably don't want him as your best or second-best player, but he's also an overqualified No. 6-7 hitter who brings so much else to the table."
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Guardians land Bubic
The Cleveland Guardians have agreed to a free-agent contract with left-hander Kris Bubic, Sportsnet reports. The contract is for $17.5 million over one year, according to ESPN. Bubic, 29, made nine starts for the Kansas City Royals last season, and after the trade to the Los Angeles Dodgers, he was used out of the bullpen. Bubic has an outlier fastball thanks to its rise and his unusual release point, and he's an interesting "ceiling" candidate in the rotation. However, his substantial history of injuries may mean he's best used out of the bullpen. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Tigers add Kim
The Detroit Tigers have added infield depth by agreeing to terms with Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year, $5 million free agent contract, ESPN reports. Kim, 31, is coming off a rough partial season with the Atlanta Braves, but he has a more palatable OPS+ of 91 for his career. He's been a primary shortstop in recent years and also has significant time spent at second base and third base. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Twins still looking for help on the marketEven after achieving a reunion with veteran starting pitcher Sonny Gray, the Minnesota Twins are still looking to fortify their roster for a return to contention in 2027. The club still hopes to make one more significant addition this offseason and add another player who may not grab as many headlines, the Athletic reports. Atop the wishlist are a first baseman or a second baseman and another lefty reliever. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Mets may be eyeing more rotation additionsEven after the splash addition of Skubal, the Mets may not be done adding starting pitchers in the service of a rebound season in 2027. On that front, the Mets may be interested in adding a starting pitcher on a short-term deal for next season, the Athletic reports. That would likely limit them to the back half of the market, especially with so many bigger names reaching agreements.

        The fourth edition of the College Football Playoff Rankings was released Tuesday night, and on the heels of a chaotic Week 12 that brought its fair share of upsets, we have some big changes among the top four. Following its first loss of the season, previously fourth-ranked UCLA has fallen five spots to No. 9, leaving the Bruins in a potential must-win situation on Saturday against USC to remain in the field. UCLA coach Bob Chesney shared optimism Monday that quarterback Ty Dieffenbach could return this weekend following a lower-body injury suffered against Michigan, so it's clear the selection committee took that into account.Texas has pushed into the top four following UCLA's exit, coming in at No. 3. The Longhorns, who have won five straight since consecutive losses last month to Oklahoma and Florida, can clinch a bid in the SEC Championship Game next weekend with a win over Texas A&M and a loss by Alabama or Tennessee.Georgia held steady in the No. 1 spot after yet another convincing win, this time over South Carolina, while clinching a berth in the SEC Championship Game in the process. Utah, the FBS's lone unbeaten team, checks in again at the No. 2 spot after a thrilling win over TCU. Meanwhile, Notre Dame hopped into the No. 4 spot after Alabama dropped to No. 6. Tennessee rounds out the top five -- a course correction by the committee, with the Volunteers holding not only the better resume but a head-to-head win over the Tide. 
For the first time this season, no Group of Six team was ranked in the top 25, this coming after Boise State was upset by San Diego State in Week 12. Should the Broncos take care of business this weekend and in the Pac-12 title rematch with the Aztecs next Friday, then they'll be in line for the 12-seed in the field. College Football Playoff Rankings, Nov. 24~ First-round byeGeorgia (10-1) ~Utah (11-0) ~Texas (9-2) ~Notre Dame (10-1) ~Tennessee (9-2)Alabama (9-2)Miami (10-1)Wake Forest (10-1)UCLA (10-1)BYU (9-2)Texas Tech (10-1)Oregon (8-3)Iowa (9-2)Indiana (9-2)USC (8-3)Arizona (8-3)Oklahoma (7-4)Houston (8-3)Louisville (8-3)Florida (7-4)Ohio State (7-4)Ole Miss (7-4)Missouri (7-4)Washington (7-4)Nebraska (7-4)Behind the top-four shakeupFor the first time in two weeks, the selection committee has altered its top four with Texas' arrival following UCLA's first loss of the season at Michigan. The move to No. 3 for the Longhorns is substantial because they're likely going to be playing top-ranked Georgia in the final SEC Championship Game on Dec. 5. Last season, the selection committee did not dock Alabama for losing to the Bulldogs in the same setting, but that could change next month if 7th-ranked Miami gets Malachi Toney back and wins the ACC, or perhaps Notre Dame further impresses after the smoke clears from rivalry weekend and pushes ahead further.The Longhorns hold a nation-leading seven wins over FBS teams with winning records this season, but unfortunately, they won't get a resume boost with a victory at Texas A&M on Friday. A loss, however, would tank this week's advantageous bump.
Previously third-seeded Alabama moved to No. 6 given the Crimson Tide's noticeable resume hit. Alabama's three best SEC wins this fall — Kentucky, South Carolina and LSU — are a combined 1-8 in November and winless over the last two weeks of play. The Crimson Tide have three victories over Power Four teams above .500 on the season, half of Georgia's total and one fewer than unbeaten and second-ranked Utah.Tennessee is a big mover to the coveted No. 5 spot, finally leaping Alabama for the first time.The buzz for weeks has been the "pod" dialogue involving Alabama and Tennessee, who has four such victories, including a 16-point win over the Crimson Tide. And in terms of "ranked" wins, defined as victories over teams currently ranked by the selection committee, Alabama has none this season after LSU, South Carolina and Kentucky all left the rankings. 
By comparison, 17th-ranked Oklahoma has three in the same conference.Notre Dame moved to No. 4 this week and, given the Fighting Irish's head-to-head win over Miami and the Hurricanes three spots back of Marcus Freeman's team, it's difficult to foresee a slide back. The selection committee clearly respects the win over the Hurricanes earlier this month.Committee rewarding hot teams (as they should)Entering rivalry week, Texas has won five straight against SEC competition since a pair of three-point losses last month to Oklahoma and Florida, while 8th-ranked Wake Forest rose for the third straight reveal after debuting at No. 16 on Nov. 3. Notice, too, that the selection committee did not dock the Demon Deacons for the season-ending injury to leading rusher Ty Clark. While he's a significant loss, it's not as impactful on the team's value as, say, quarterback Gio Lopez going down would be.Since losing to one-loss Miami in Week 3, Wake Forest has beaten its seven ACC opponents by an average of 31.7 points per game. The Demon Deacons are 14.5-point favorites in Saturday's finale against Duke, but do have to deal with ACC leading rusher Nate Sheppard. Miami beat Duke earlier this month, 36-25.
No. 12 Oregon is making its move, too. During this four-game winning streak that has extended in November, the Ducks have jumped from No. 23 to No. 16 to No. 13 and now this. If Oregon beats Washington on Saturday and wins the Big Ten championship next weekend to clinch an auto-bid, the Ducks will become the only team in the 12-team era to debut beyond No. 18 in the initial rankings and still appear in the field.Big Ten needs resuscitation Curt Cignetti can say what he wants about his team's weekly grind in the Big Ten, but the basis for his argument fell flat following Indiana's loss to Washington. Indiana's slip to No. 14 means the defending national champions are likely not heading back to the CFP. The Hoosiers can still make next week's Big Ten Championship Game, but they need a win over Purdue and considerable help.The situation's equally dire for 9th-ranked UCLA, but at least the Bruins control their destiny, as Bob Chesney put it Monday before his team's five-spot fall from No. 4 after their first loss. Quarterback Ty Dieffenbach "took reps" at Tuesday's practice per Chesney, three days after he was carted off the field in overtime at Michigan.
Much has been said about UCLA's potential Florida State situation if Dieffenbach's injury was season-ending, like what happened to Jordan Travis and the Seminoles in 2023. It appears, however, that UCLA's QB1 might suit up for Saturday's contest with USC. A loss puts the Bruins on the bubble, while a win solidifies a berth in the Big Ten title game.The Big Ten has won three consecutive national championships, but that doesn't matter during the selection committee's deliberations since this league has faded late this season. Outside of Oregon and 13th-ranked Iowa's solid play this month, No. 21 Ohio State's playoff hopes are basically over, and the Bruins and Hoosiers are no longer in favorable positions.While unlikely, there's a chance this is a single-bid league on Selection Sunday, quite shocking considering the league produced eight teams inside the preseason top 25.
